Yuan-Ping Pang pointed drug designers at a fresh target for stopping malaria mosquitoes in a 2006 paper. Acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme in the insect nervous system, and poisons that block it are a main class of insecticides. Resistance and harm to other species limit the old compounds, which hit a well-known site on the enzyme.

Pang identified a novel target site on acetylcholinesterase, a fresh place where a control agent might bind. A new site raises the hope of insecticides that kill malaria-carrying mosquitoes while sparing humans and helpful insects, and that work even where resistance has beaten the old sprays. For a disease spread only by these mosquitoes, better control tools save lives directly.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d58: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 26, 1943, as the Moscow Conference neared its close. His message is Document 58 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. October 26 was a crowded day in the volume, full of letters between capitals and conference rooms. The record for this one gives the date and the names and nothing narrower. It survives in the Foreign Relations series with the rest of that day's traffic.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d158: An editorial note dated May 5, 1943 stands as Document 158 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, far from the volume's opening where its twin note sits. Editorial notes in the Foreign Relations series mark seams where the editors joined bodies of papers, and this one opens the Moscow Conference section that follows. Reading it tells the reader whose files the next papers came from and how the editors handled them.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d258:
The Chinese record of a Cairo conversation between President Roosevelt and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek is introduced by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. No official American record of the talk was found, and none appears to have been prepared, so the editors print a Chinese summary instead.

The Chinese government held the record in its own files, had it translated from Chinese, and gave leave for its printing in 1957. The note also flags gaps in the Log. The Log lists the Chiangs, Hopkins, and Colonel Elliott Roosevelt as dinner guests. The colonel's own account gives no sign he attended. Topics his book adds, missing from the Chinese summary, include a coalition government for China, British rights in Shanghai and Canton, and the future of Malaya, Burma, and India.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d358:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the first meeting between President Roosevelt and Marshal Stalin, at Tehran on 28 November 1943 at three in the afternoon. The two leaders had never met, and Roosevelt opens with pleasure: he has tried for a long time to bring this about.

Stalin blames the delay on military business. Then he gives a frank front report. The Soviets have lost Zhitomir and are about to lose Korosten. They hold the initiative elsewhere, but can attack only in the Ukraine. Roosevelt says he wishes he could pull thirty or forty German divisions off the Eastern front, a question he wants Tehran to address. Talk turns to postwar trade and a surplus merchant fleet for Russia. It turns then to China, whose fighting Stalin faults on its leaders. Last comes Lebanon, which Roosevelt blames wholly on de Gaulle's committee.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d458: Number 458 in the Cairo-Tehran volume is an editorial note. Department historians use the note form to speak in their own voice. They add facts, explain references, and point to other documents. The record here covers the Allied conferences of late 1943. Strategy for Europe and Asia dominated those meetings. So did early arguments about the postwar world. The note gives readers footing before the papers resume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d558:
A second Churchill message to President Roosevelt is dated March 4, 1944, hard on the heels of the first. The pair continues the dense exchange of that week. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Two messages a day, two days running, tells its own story about March 1944: the invasion was three months off, and every theater's claims collided in the leaders' in-trays. Churchill separated his subjects into single papers, and Roosevelt answered in kind. For readers, this message helps reconstruct a week of alliance management at full stretch, preserved because the State Department printed the conference volumes generously.
frus-1944-quebec-d58:
President Roosevelt answered Prime Minister Churchill on September 6, 1944. The reply appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, among the final pre-conference exchanges.

Roosevelt's answers that week kept the welcome warm and the American positions intact. He faced a guest who would argue hard for Britain's share in the Pacific war and for generous aid terms, and the President's letters prepared his ground. For readers, this message closes the transatlantic preparation: within a week the two men would be talking across a table in Quebec City instead of across an ocean.
frus-1944-quebec-d158:
Admiral Leahy wrote to Hull for the Joint Chiefs on August 29, 1944, giving the military view of French participation in the war against Japan. Indochina, the letter stresses, lies in the China theater and is an area of American strategic responsibility. It quotes the views Chiang Kai-shek expressed at Sextant on how the two theaters should divide Thailand and Indochina.

From a military standpoint, the chiefs concurred with the British proposals. One exception mattered: French participation in planning political warfare should be restricted to the Southeast Asia Command area. The letter also counsels recognizing French desires about Indochina where consistent with American policy, with extent and timing kept under continuing review.
frus-1944-quebec-d258:
Control of the strategic bomber forces in Europe is addressed in C.C.S. 520/4, the United States Chiefs' paper of September 13, 1944. With Allied armies now on the continent, the wartime arrangement under Eisenhower's direction was ending. The Americans agreed in principle with joint control by the RAF's Deputy Chief of the Air Staff and the commander of the United States Strategic Air Forces in Europe.

Those two officers, Bottomley and Spaatz, would act jointly for Portal and Arnold as agents of the Combined Chiefs. The Americans found the British draft directive inadequate in several respects, however, and attached a revised directive of their own. The Combined Chiefs approved it, as amended, the following day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d58:
From Moscow on 16 January 1945, Ambassador Averell Harriman reported to President Roosevelt on where the American party would sleep at Yalta. His top secret telegram is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. It deals with rooms, not strategy.

Harriman says Roosevelt will stay in the Livadia palace, the czar's former summer home. The site has one building of 21 rooms, one of 41, and a third once used by guards. Space for the enlarged military party is still unsure, so he is asking the Soviets for more rooms. The support ship Catoctin, he notes, can only be based at Sevastopol.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d158:
Stalin answered Roosevelt on Poland on 29 December 1944, and the answer closed the door. His message, received in Washington in translation, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. He had the President's note of the middle of the month in hand.

hansard-admission-of-baron-de-rothschild:

swedenborg-heaven-and-hell-1758:

swedenborg-heaven-hell-1758:

herodotus-histories-rawlinson-1858:

starkey-pyrotechny-asserted-1658:

linnaeus-systema-naturae-vol1-1758:

holmes-autocrat-1858:

marguerite-de-valois-memoirs-1658:

comte-catechism-1858:

Prime Minister Suzuki of Japan spoke at a press conference on 28 July 1945. His words gave the world's first public sign of Tokyo's answer to the Potsdam Declaration, issued two days before. The statement reached Washington fast and was read there as a refusal.

Suzuki used a word, often rendered as killing the terms with silent contempt, that hardened Allied views. Whether he meant flat rejection or a wish to wait for Moscow, the effect was the same. The summit's leaders took Japan's answer as no. This statement is that answer in its public form, a hinge on which the war's last weeks turned.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1358:

Allen's Near Eastern and African affairs office kept a steady file of papers flowing to Dunn during the conference. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Dunn sat close to the center of the American effort at Potsdam, so papers addressed to him reached a man who could act. The Allen notes show a regional bureau working its questions into the summit's crowded agenda. For readers tracing Middle East policy in 1945, the Allen papers are a thread worth following. It runs from start to end of the volume's closing section.
frus-1945-50-intel-d58:

It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Staff officers keep committees alive: they call the meetings, circulate the drafts, and chase the members' views. Brownell's memorandum shows that machinery turning in December, weeks after the Lovett report. Readers might pass over such a paper, but it marks something real, the refusal of a hard question to die. The intelligence design was still being argued in committee rooms while the secretaries settled its outline above.
frus-1945-50-intel-d158: A memorandum dated 28 June 1946 was prepared for the Secretary of State's Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Langer). frus-1945-50-intel-d258:

It is document 258 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.

Reports were the heavy guns of paper work: slower than a memo, but built to end an argument. The replies it drew, kept near it in the files, show how the findings stood up to attack. frus-1861-d58:
On 1 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams at the London legation. The letter is document 58 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

July opened with Congress called to meet and the armies near Manassas. Seward's first of July letter keeps faith with the plan set in spring. It guided Adams through the weeks just before Bull Run, when a quick Union win still seemed within reach. Congress met on 4 July and voted men and money, which backed Seward's bold tone abroad. Men and money voted at home were the facts that gave his words abroad their weight.
frus-1861-d158:
On 21 October 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to William Dayton. It is document 158 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The paired form appears in the Paris file as in the London one. Each letter owns its point and its answer. Together they show how a single day's French business could fill two files and still leave the desk clear. Two files, two answers: the habit kept replies swift and the record clean. A clear desk at day's end was Seward's small, daily victory over the war.
frus-1861-d258:

It was written in the autumn of the war's first year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d58:

It was printed as Document 58 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d158:
Document 158, dated 10 October 1862, carries a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It sits in the long Great Britain section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Three days earlier, William Gladstone had said in a speech at Newcastle that the South had made a nation. Words Union men read as a push toward British backing for the Confederacy. Adams had to answer that mood in London. Seward's steady mail, of which this letter is part, armed him with Washington's position week after week. Seward trusted Adams's calm judgment and rarely overruled the man on the spot.
frus-1862-d258:
William L. Dayton reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 18 March 1862, in a letter printed as Document 258 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton represented the United States in Paris as its minister.

Mid-March brought the Union's Peninsula campaign toward Richmond just as France was deciding to go it alone in Mexico after its allies pulled back. Dayton reported on a court balancing two American ventures at once. His letters are a chief source for how Napoleon III's government weighed the Confederate cause against its Mexican design that spring. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d358:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, addressed Henri Mercier on 20 February 1862 in a letter printed as Document 358 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It closed a run of three Seward letters to the French minister in two weeks.

Late February 1862 was a bright moment for the Union, with Fort Donelson fallen and Nashville about to follow. Seward negotiated from strength that month, a fact foreign legations registered. His letters to Mercier in this window show a secretary using good news as diplomatic capital while it lasted. Cases in this channel often mixed the war at home with French designs in Mexico.
frus-1862-d458:

Motley wrote as McClellan stood before Richmond and Europe waited to see if the Confederate capital would fall. Austria, busy with its own Italian and German problems, kept a strict and chilly neutrality. His report told Washington how the war's climax looked from the Danube. Letters like this one, from a minor post in the great question, still mattered. Seward's map of Europe had to be complete. Vienna's silence was itself a fact worth recording.
frus-1862-d558:
On 18 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Shelton Sanford in Brussels. The instruction is Document 558 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Seward wrote the day after Antietam, in the same mid-September round that reached Madrid, Vienna, and The Hague. Sanford's Brussels post gave him a window on French and British thinking through King Leopold's wide family web. Orders to such a post mixed the government's line with requests for what the minister was hearing. The dispatch shows Seward gathering Europe's reaction to the autumn crisis through his most connected small-post minister, even before the battle's result was fully known.
frus-1862-d658:

In the last weeks of 1861 Seward sent Pruyn a run of letters, each adding to the charge the new envoy would carry. They dealt with the work of the legation and the stance the United States meant to keep in Japan. This one is a mid-run piece, useful chiefly as part of the full set that sent Pruyn off with his orders in hand.
frus-1863p1-d58:

Seward wrote to keep Adams aimed at the standing aims: no British aid for the South, no warships out of British yards. It is a hinge piece, joining the winter run to what came before.
frus-1863p1-d158:

A three-letter day late in April shows the ship question still filling the post's plate. Adams gave the yards, the talks, and the press each a sheet. This one opens the set of 17 April. In the volume's long London run, the day is one more crest in a spring of crests. Each charts Britain's slow turn from the South's hopes.

It stands as document 358 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d458:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington directed a letter to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 11 April 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d558:
In the flow of wartime mail, William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 8 June 1863. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d658:
The 9 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.

Jun Wu, Thomas J. Klein, and Marek Mlodzik studied signal receptors in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2004. Frizzled receptors pass Wnt signals, which guide growth and body pattern. The authors tracked where in the cell these receptors sit, a trait set by their inner tails.

Where a receptor sits decides which signals it can send. The team's work shows the tail acts like an address label, sending the receptor to the right cell compartment. That placement then tunes the strength and kind of signal that follows. The study adds a layer to how Wnt signaling is controlled, a pathway that is central to development and often goes wrong in cancer.
plos-pbio-0020258:
Jennifer L. Nemhauser, Todd C. Mockler, and Joanne Chory studied plant hormone cross-talk in PLOS Biology in 2004. Plants use hormones called brassinosteroids and auxin to guide growth. Both affect stems, roots, and leaves, so their signals must be coordinated rather than sent in isolation.

Using the model plant Arabidopsis, the team showed the two pathways lean on each other. Many genes respond to both signals, and blocking one changes the effect of the other. That interdependence is a design rule for plant growth control. It matters for farming, since tweaks to one hormone path will ripple into the other. The paper helped move plant science past single-hormone thinking.
plos-pone-0000158:
Paul D. Waters, Gauthier Dobigny, Peter J. Waddell, and colleagues published this evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. LINE-1 is a jumping gene, a stretch of DNA that copies itself into new spots in the genome. It makes up a large share of mammal DNA. The authors trace its history across the major clades of placental mammals.

By comparing LINE-1 across species, the team reconstructs when this element was active and how it spread. The story helps explain why mammal genomes differ so much in size and content. It also gives a backdrop for the many gene changes that jumping elements cause, for better and worse.
plos-pone-0000258:
Michael J. Angilletta, Robbie S. Wilson, Amanda C. Niehaus, and colleagues published this urban ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007, under the heading of urban physiology. It reports that city ants possess high heat tolerance, handling temperatures that would trouble their rural kin. Cities run warmer than the countryside, a heat island effect ants must cope with.

Urban animals are evolving under new pressures, and heat is one of the sharpest. The authors compare the heat tolerance of city ants with what the species normally shows. The result is an early data point in the study of how wildlife adapts to city life.
plos-pone-0000358:
Justin D. Blethrow, Chao Tang, Changhui Deng, and colleagues published this proteomics methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents a modular mass spectrometric tool for analyzing protein complexes. The tool reads what the complexes are made of, and how their parts are phosphorylated, chemically tagged in ways that switch activity. The tool's modules can be combined as needed.

Protein complexes run the cell, and their tags change with conditions. A modular instrument workflow makes such analysis more routine and flexible. The paper is a methods contribution to proteomics, the large-scale study of proteins, as it moved from listing parts to mapping their states.
plos-pone-0000458:
Jennifer Hartt Meyers and colleagues studied how HIV weakens a specialized immune cell, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are the body's champion producers of interferon, an alarm signal against viruses. The team measured the impact of HIV on these cells' survival and on their antiviral activity.

If HIV kills or disables the very cells meant to raise the alarm, the immune system starts the fight already handicapped. Documenting that damage helps explain why HIV infection so often becomes chronic. It also points to protecting or restoring these cells as a possible treatment strategy, alongside drugs that attack the virus directly.
plos-pone-0000558:
Yuri B. Yurov and colleagues examined chromosome errors in the developing human brain, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Aneuploidy means a cell carries the wrong number of chromosomes; confined chromosomal mosaicism means only some cells in the tissue are affected. The team documented both in brain development.

The brain was long assumed to be chromosomally uniform. Finding mosaicism there raises questions about how much variation is normal and whether abnormal patches contribute to disease. Counting chromosomes cell by cell in developing tissue is slow work, but it set reference points for later claims about the mosaic brain.
plos-pone-0000658:
Andrei I. Ivanov, Moshe Bachar, Brian A. Babbin and colleagues singled out one motor protein at the seams between surface cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Epithelial sheets form barriers, and their strength depends on the apical junctional complex, built from tight and adherens junctions. Actin filaments beneath the surface regulate that complex. Myosin II, a major actin motor, was already implicated.

The team reports a unique role for one form, nonmuscle myosin heavy chain IIA, in regulating these apical junctions. Unique means the other forms do not simply cover for it. Barrier breakdown drives gut and skin diseases, so knowing which motor holds the seams matters.
plos-pone-0000758:
Christophe Fraser developed simpler ways to estimate how fast a new epidemic is spreading, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Reproduction numbers, the average number of people infected by a typical case, play a central role in tracking outbreaks. His aim was methods simple enough to be applied as an epidemic emerges, when data are thin and decisions cannot wait.

Fraser separates individual and household reproduction numbers. Spread within households behaves differently from spread between them, and mixing the two distorts forecasts. Estimating both gives a clearer picture of whether an outbreak will take off. Methods papers like this become the toolbox reached for in the first weeks of a crisis.
plos-pone-0000858:
Li-Tzu Chen, Tzu-Ping Ko, Yu-Wei Chang and colleagues probed five charged building blocks in an archaeal DNA repair protein, for PLOS ONE in 2007. RecA family proteins run an ATP-dependent DNA strand exchange, in which a single-stranded DNA filament finds and pairs with a matching double-stranded sequence. Despite more than 20 years of effort, the molecular mechanism of homology pairing and strand exchange was still not fully known.

Their RadA protein comes from archaea, microbes with ancient molecular machinery. The five conserved positively charged residues sit in the L1 and N-terminal DNA-binding motifs. Structural and functional analyses of exactly those residues test how the protein grips DNA during the search for a match.
plos-pone-0000958:
Alexander Statnikov, Chun Li and Constantin Aliferis studied how environment, genes and analysis choices can mislead a cancer gene hunt, in PLOS ONE in 2007. New genotyping tools let researchers scan the whole genome for variants tied to disease. Early studies suggested panels of markers could flag esophageal cancer risk.

The authors warn that pitfalls in data analysis, and tangled effects of environment and genetics, can inflate such claims. Their paper is a caution worked through a real case. Gene wide studies are powerful, but only when the statistics respect how messy human data are. The work is aimed at everyone building risk panels.
plos-pone-0001058:
Naohiro Kawamura, Fumitaka Kugimiya, Yasushi Oshima and colleagues studied a signaling protein's role on both sides of bone turnover, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bone mass is held by balance: osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts resorb it, under many local and body wide controls. Akt is one of the key serine threonine kinases in that control web.

The team examined Akt1 in both cell types. A single protein acting in builder and demolisher alike could coordinate the two, keeping turnover matched. Bone diseases from osteoporosis to arthritis involve that match failing. Knowing which Akt form sits where helps target treatment without upsetting the other side.
plos-pone-0001158:
The prion protein is famous for its role in transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, diseases such as scrapie and BSE. Yet its normal job in the body is still unclear. Marius Lötscher and colleagues found an unexpected one in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Using histology, immunochemistry, and PCR-based methods in mice, they linked the protein to immune defense.

The team reports that induced prion protein controls retroviruses that the immune system activates in the mouse spleen. In other words, when the spleen's defenses switch on, prion protein helps keep resident retroviruses in check. That gives the protein a concrete normal function to set beside its disease role.
plos-pone-0001258:
Long QT syndrome is an inherited heart rhythm disorder that can kill without warning. John Bankston and colleagues report the case of a newborn carrying a new mutation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The mutation sits in SCN5A, the gene for the heart's main sodium channel, and caused the variant called LQT-3.

The authors describe the de novo mutation as novel and lethal, with distinct molecular pharmacology and a distinct therapeutic response. De novo means it appeared fresh in the child, not inherited. Working out how this channel variant answers to drugs guided treatment of a very young patient.
plos-pone-0001358:
Arcobacter butzleri is a bacterium found in human clinical cases, a member of the epsilon subdivision of the Proteobacteria. William Miller and colleagues present its complete genome sequence in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. It is a close relative of established pathogens such as Campylobacter jejuni and Helicobacter pylori.

The authors worked out the full genome sequence of the human clinical isolate. A complete sequence shows what the bacterium can do, and which of its genes might help it cause disease. For a little-studied relative of two major pathogens, the genome is the reference everything else builds on.
plos-pone-0001458:
Frank Schweitzer and Robert Mach published a 2008 PLOS ONE paper on the spread of giving. When a cause takes off, gifts can surge like an outbreak. The pair show that a disease spread model fits this surge well. In their frame, word of a cause passes from person to person like a germ.

Herding plays a key role, as donors watch what the crowd does through the media. The model uses a shared field that stands for that media pull over time. A good fit lets groups forecast how a drive will rise and fade. It also hints at when a push will do the most good.
plos-pone-0001558:
Michiel van Boven and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on when people will take flu drugs. Drugs that curb viruses hold promise for new ills such as bird flu and SARS. But the drugs are not free of harm, so people weigh gain against risk. The team modeled when self interest and group gain pull in unlike ways.

In their model, what pays for one person can fail the group as a whole. That gap can stall a drug drive that needs wide uptake to work. Plans must thus align the two, with clear rules and fair access. The work frames a social snag that pure drug science cannot solve.
plos-pone-0001658:
Juliette Salvaing, Anja C. Nagel, Emmanuèle Mouchel-Vielh, and their co-authors studied two gene-control proteins in the fruit fly in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Polycomb group proteins keep genes switched off over the long term, while trithorax group proteins keep them on. Together they hold gene patterns steady through development, above all for Hox genes, which set body layout.

The paper centers on Corto, a protein that works with both camps, and its interaction with Cyclin G. The full text gives the binding tests, the fly genetics, and where the two proteins meet. Their meeting point links the on-off memory system to a protein better known from cell growth. It may explain how Corto fine-tunes gene patterns as the fly develops.
plos-pone-0001758:
Nuo Yang, Jia Huang, Joel Greshock, and their co-authors studied how an ovarian cancer gene is switched on in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. PIK3CA is boosted, amplified, or mutated in ovarian and other cancers, making it a promising drug target. How it gets over-activated in living tumors was unclear.

The team reports that NF-κB, a master inflammation switch, transcriptionally regulates PIK3CA in the ovarian cancer microenvironment, the tissue setting around the tumor. The full text gives the gene activity tests and the binding evidence. If inflammation switches on a growth gene, then anti-inflammatory strategies or NF-κB blockers could complement drugs aimed at PIK3CA itself.
plos-pone-0001858:
Robin M. D. Beck, Henk Godthelp, Vera Weisbecker, and their co-authors described the oldest marsupial fossils of Australia in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. New skull and body fossils come from the early Eocene Tingamarra Local Fauna. The team refers them to Djarthia murgonensis, known before only from broken tooth remains.

The new finds show Djarthia is a member of a distinct marsupial group. Its kinship bears on how marsupials reached Australia and spread across it. The full text gives the fossil accounts and the family analysis. The marsupials of Australia are a textbook case of evolution in isolation, and their oldest fossils anchor the timeline of that story.
plos-pone-0001958:
Myriam Rai and co-authors tested a drug fix for a nerve illness in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The illness, Friedreich ataxia, is passed down in families and harms both nerves and the heart. It stems from too little frataxin, a protein that works in the cell's power units, caused by a swollen repeat in the frataxin gene.

The team gave HDAC inhibitors, drugs that loosen the chemical marks that mute genes, to a mouse model of the illness. As the title states, the drugs corrected the frataxin shortage in the mice. If a muted gene can be coaxed back on, a drug path opens for an illness with no cure.
plos-pone-0002058:
Steven Schutzer and co-authors read the genome of a weakened form of a biothreat bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Burkholderia mallei causes glanders, which can be lethal in humans and animals, and it is little studied. Safety rules for listed agents have hampered research with it in many labs.

The team used whole genome sequencing to characterize a clinically attenuated strain, one that no longer causes full disease. If its genome proves it is truly weakened, the strain could be excluded from select agent lists. That would let more labs study glanders safely.
plos-pone-0002158:
Hendrik Harms, Konstantin Prass, Christian Meisel, and co-authors ran a clinical trial on preventing infection after stroke, published in PLOS ONE in 2008. Pneumonia is a leading cause of death after a major stroke. In mice, giving the antibiotic moxifloxacin early had prevented post-stroke infections, lowered deaths, and improved recovery.

The team tested the same idea in people with acute ischemic stroke, where a clot blocks blood flow to the brain. Patients were assigned by chance to preventive antibiotic therapy or standard care. Trials like this one decide whether a result seen in animals can be turned into a routine step that saves lives in the ward.
plos-pone-0002258:
Alison McGuigan, Derek Bruzewicz, Ana Glavan, and co-authors described a way to grow cells in tiny gel blocks, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cells behave differently on flat plastic than in the three-dimensional world of the body. Flat culture is still the most common method in biology, while 3D culture lacks a standard, easy form.

The team used replica molding to make sub-millimeter gel modules with cells sealed inside. The small blocks can be handled, stacked, and combined like building pieces. A simple standard for 3D culture could bring lab results closer to how cells truly behave inside tissues.
plos-pone-0002358:
Domingo Ojer Tsakiridu and co-authors surveyed factors linked to induced abortion among sex workers in Asturias, Spain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Their aim was to find what circumstances go together with having had an induced abortion in this group. The health needs of this group are often missed by standard services.

The team ran a cross-sectional study using a self-completion questionnaire answered by 212 women who attended the region's three sexually transmitted infection clinics. Mapping the factors that cluster with abortion helps those clinics target contraception advice, testing, and support to the women at highest risk.
plos-pone-0002458:
A research team led by Perfettini reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Jean-Luc Perfettini, Roberta Nardacci, Mehdi Bourouba, and others. Its subject is critical Involvement of the ATM-Dependent DNA Damage Response in the Apoptotic Demise of HIV-1-Elicited Syncytia. DNA damage can activate the oncosuppressor protein ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM), which phosphorylates the histone H2AX within characteristic DNA damage foci.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002558:
Work from Nishimura and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Tomoko Nishimura, Tamaki Ishima, Masaomi Iyo, and others. Its subject is potentiation of Nerve Growth Factor-Induced Neurite Outgrowth by Fluvoxamine. The title goes on to note role of Sigma-1 Receptors, IP 3 Receptors and Cellular Signaling Pathways. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have been widely used and are a major therapeutic advance in psychopharmacology.

However, their pharmacology is quite heterogeneous. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002658:
Pawan Gupta led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was PKCε stimulated arginine methylation of RIP140 for its Nuclear-Cytoplasmic export in adipocyte differentiation. Receptor interacting protein 140 (RIP140) is a versatile transcriptional co-repressor that plays roles in diverse metabolic processes including fat accumulation in adipocytes. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002758:
Céline Lafourcade led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was regulation of the V-ATPase along the endocytic pathway occurs through reversible subunit association and membrane localization. The catalog record names Céline Lafourcade first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

Luminal pH thereby regulates important processes such as the release of internalized ligands from their receptor or the activation of lysosomal enzymes. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002858:
Morten Ruhwald led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was improving T-Cell assays for the diagnosis of latent TB infection: potential of a diagnostic test based on IP-10. Authorship is credited in the record to Morten Ruhwald and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. There is a need for simple tools such as the M.tuberculosis specific IFN-γ release assays (IGRA) to improve diagnosis of M.tuberculosis -infection in children. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002958:
Sofia Kring, Claus Holst, Esther Zimmermann and co-authors studied the fatness gene FTO across a wide range of body fat in 2008. A common variant in FTO, labeled rs9939609, is linked to total body fatness. What it does for fat placement and related metabolic traits was less clear.

The team checked the variant against abdominal and peripheral fat and obesity-linked traits in middle-aged men spanning a broad range of fatness. Published in PLOS ONE, the design shows whether the gene's effect grows, fades, or changes form as fatness rises. Such detail refines a headline gene link.
plos-pone-0003058:
José Cuevas, Manuela Torres-Puente, Nuria Jiménez-Hernández and co-authors tracked hepatitis C virus change around therapy in 2008. They analyzed selective forces on two genome regions thought to be involved in response to combined interferon plus ribavirin therapy. One region holds three hypervariable parts of the envelope E2 protein.

Comparing virus before and after combined therapy shows which sites selection pressed hardest. Published in PLOS ONE, such maps help explain treatment failure and resistance. Hepatitis C evolves fast within a patient, so therapy must be judged against a moving target. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003158:
K. Bretonnel Cohen, Martha Palmer and Lawrence Hunter study verb forms in biomedical writing in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They present data from the PennBioIE corpus on how common domain-specific verbs change their argument structure, and how their related noun forms behave. Alternation is the linguistics term for such shifts in the surface form of a verb.

Readers learn how biomedical verbs and their nominalizations vary in real text. That detail sounds narrow, but it matters for computer systems that mine medical papers for facts. Better handling of these forms means fewer errors when machines extract who did what to what.
plos-pone-0003258:
Amelia Cimmino, Rosanna Capasso, Fabbri Muller and colleagues study a repair enzyme in blood vessel cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Natural proteins undergo deamidation of certain asparagine residues in the body on their own, forming isoaspartyl residues. Deamidated, isomerized molecules are changed in both shape and how they work. The enzyme protein isoaspartate methyltransferase acts on such damage.

The title reports that this enzyme prevents apoptosis induced by oxidative stress in endothelial cells, with a role for Bcl-Xl deamidation and methylation. Readers see protein repair linked to cell survival under stress. Vessel lining protection matters in ageing and blood vessel disease.
plos-pone-0003358:
Jochen Brumm, Elizabeth Conibear, Wyeth W. Wasserman and colleagues present a method to find gene modules in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A central problem in systems biology research is identification and extension of biological modules, groups of genes or proteins participating in a common cellular process or physical complex. There is a persistent need for practical, principled methods to infer such modules from data.

Their approach discovers and expands gene modules by seeking isolated groups in a random graph process. Readers get an algorithm that grows modules from seeds while testing against randomness. Module maps help turn gene lists into working biological units.
plos-pone-0007458: Diatoms are ocean algae that build glass shells from silicon, and this study read the activity of nearly every gene in one species, Phaeodactylum tricornutum, to learn how. The researchers found silicon transport is controlled at multiple levels, with a network of transporter genes responding to supply. Understanding this system matters because diatoms drive a huge share of ocean life.
plos-pone-0007558: Prisons concentrate people at high risk for HIV, and this 2006 census analysis found inmates and recent releasees still carry a disproportionate share of America's epidemic — though the share was declining. Because so many pass through the system, the authors argue correctional facilities remain a critical place to test, treat, and prevent.
plos-pone-0007658: Even on successful HIV therapy, traces of virus linger — and this study links that residual viremia to ongoing immune activation. In patients whose immune systems recovered poorly, low-level virus tracked with restless T cells. The finding suggests the lingering virus is not harmless background noise.
plos-pone-0007758: Does news coverage of opioids fuel the crisis or just report it? This study compared the volume of media reports with opioid death rates over time. The temporal association suggests coverage and mortality move together — raising hard questions about the media's role.
plos-pone-0007858: Monkey food fads got a peer-pressure test. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Dindo's team showed capuchins copy their group's foraging habits. Wild apes flaunt rich traditions. The copycat pattern was mapped. The test feeds primate culture science.
plos-pone-0007958: Large chunks of DNA vary between populations. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Li and colleagues mapped copy number variation across the genome in Caucasian and Asian populations. Beyond single-letter changes, whole segments get duplicated or deleted. Charting their ethnic patterns reveals a neglected layer of human genetic diversity.
plos-pone-0008058: The case for tiny 'nanobacteria' in blood fell apart under chemistry. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Wu and colleagues showed that the strange granules are just complexes of blood proteins, fetuin-A and albumin, with calcium minerals. These specks had been claimed as a new form of life, but they form on their own when proteins both block and seed mineral growth. The team demonstrated the two-step process in the lab. With a plain chemical explanation in hand, there is no need to invoke living nanobacteria.
plos-pone-0008158: Eye fluid was screened for the immune signals behind blinding eye ills. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Yoshimura's team sampled the vitreous gel from 345 patients with diabetic eye ills such as macular swelling. The team read out dozens of immune messengers to see which run highest in each ill. The signal patterns point to the drivers of each ill. The map gives drug hunters targets for cooling the eye's harmful immune flare-ups.
plos-pone-0008258: A visual trick got a brain-echo predictor. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Kessler's team tied the flash-lag illusion to motor resonance. Moving bodies warp perceived timing. The echo link was measured. The predictor feeds vision science.
plos-pone-0008358: Adult bones were found remembering their youth. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Rawlinson's team showed rat bones keep regionalized gene-expression markers from development. The skull resists the bone loss that plagues limbs. The lingering markers may explain the contrast. The developmental memory hints at site-specific therapies.
plos-pone-0008458: Brown fat's power plants got a development timeline. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Murholm's team tracked mitochondrial DNA genes during mouse brown fat cell formation. Brown fat burns energy; white fat stores it. The gene timeline shows the burn machinery assembling. The dynamic map links mitochondria to heat production.
plos-pone-0008558: Two tumor guards' teamwork got dissected. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by McClendon's team tested how RB and p53 pathways shape DNA damage response and therapy-induced transformation in mouse cells. The duo is often lost together in cancers. Their cooperation was surprisingly murky. The dissection clarifies the partnership.
plos-pone-0008658: A brain gene's volume knob got found. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Spigoni's team showed antisense transcripts regulate Emx2 expression in mouse cortical precursors. The cortex-building transcription factor needed tuning. The antisense control was mapped. The knob reveals developmental fine-tuning.
plos-pone-0008758: A diabetes drug got a longevity bonus. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Onken and Driscoll showed metformin extends worm healthspan via AMPK, LKB1, and SKN-1, mimicking dietary restriction. The longevity pathway was mapped. The bonus informs aging research.
plos-pone-0008858: Brain channels' wandering got filmed. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Gómez-Varela's team tracked Eag1 channel lateral mobility in rat hippocampal cultures with quantum dots. The single-particle tracking was run. The film informs synapse biology.
plos-pone-0008958: A skin-tone hormone got an immune job. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Loser's team showed alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone drives cytotoxic CD8 T-cell development in mice and humans. The neuropeptide's immune role was mapped. The job informs immunology.
plos-pone-0009058: Mouse hearing got a dock-knockout timeline. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Turcan's team tracked ear growth in mice missing a key hearing dock. The stalled growth and calm-signal rise were logged. The timeline feeds hearing science.
plos-pone-0009158: Ethiopia's TB care got a cost audit. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Datiko and Lindtjørn measured the cost-effectiveness of health extension workers treating smear-positive TB. The community-care economics were run. The audit informs TB policy.
plos-pone-0009258: Mouse skin got an eczema-and-blood-disease story. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Dumortier's team showed Notch-signaling loss in skin causes dermatitis-like disease and lethal myeloproliferation. The skin-immune link was mapped. The story informs dermatology.
plos-pone-0009358: Fake-joint infections got a blood-flag check. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Piper's team checked blood flags for fake-joint infections. The flag check was logged. The flags guide re-do surgery. The check covers hips and knees.
plos-pone-0011458: Kawasaki disease strikes young children with fever and inflamed blood vessels, sometimes scarring coronary arteries. This research paper links gene variants in CCR2-CCR5 and copy numbers of CCL3L1 to the disease, its heart complications, and response to IVIG treatment in Japanese children. The genetic clues could one day help doctors predict which children need the most aggressive care.
plos-pone-0011558: Cholera's Vibrio cholerae also sickens the humble roundworm. This research paper shows the bacterium's hemolysin toxin is required to kill C. elegans, delay its development, and riddle its gut with vacuoles. The worm model turns a human pathogen's weapon into a screenable trait for studying virulence.
plos-pone-0011658: TAFI puts the brakes on clot-busting, and mice lacking it tell a cautionary tale. This research paper finds TAFI-deficient mice are prone to brain clots and ischemic stroke. The vulnerability reveals the protein's protective role in cerebral blood flow.
plos-pone-0011758: Ehrlichia germs invade white blood cells, and the immune sensor MyD88 raises the alarm. This research paper shows MyD88-driven signals help the body fight off ehrlichial infection in mice. The defense role confirms a frontline sensor doing exactly its job.
plos-pone-0011858: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors carry a gene amplification at chromosome 4q12. This research paper examines its effects on gene expression and what they mean for sunitinib treatment. The amplicon analysis points to a drug option for these rare tumors.
plos-pone-0011958: Separating male and female killifish changes how females grow. This research paper finds that housing the sexes apart boosts female body growth — but not lifespan — in the African fish Nothobranchius furzeri. The split-sex result separates growth from aging in the wild.
plos-pone-0012058: Newts can regrow their lenses — and microRNAs conduct the regrowth. This research paper studies miRNAs in newt lens regrowth, finding precise control of cell division and evidence for miRNA networking. The tiny conductors reveal regrowth's regulatory score in full detail.

Olaus Magnus, a Swedish churchman, published his great history of the northern peoples in Latin in 1555. This English version of 1658 shortens that vast work for London readers. It describes the Goths, Swedes, and Vandals, and the cold lands they came from.

Early modern Scandinavia appears here as a land of marvels. Sea serpents coil in northern waters, and mermen rise from the deep. Snow, ice, and the midnight sun shape every custom he reports. English readers of 1658 met the north mainly through such wonders. The book mixes real report with sailors' tales, and both halves are worth reading.

Gesner went down into the waters for the fourth volume of his Historiae animalium in 1558. It treats fishes and water creatures of every kind, the largest survey of sea life yet attempted in print. Rivers, lakes, and oceans all contribute their tenants to his catalogue.

Whales, sharks, and common food fish receive the same careful order. Among them stand the sea serpent and other marine monsters that sailors swore were true. Gesner weighs the reports as best his age allowed. The volume keeps one foot in marvel, and is the more fascinating for it. No earlier book had tried to hold the whole watery world at once.
hocus-pocus-junior-1658:
Hocus Pocus Junior calls itself the anatomy of legerdemain, the art of sleight of hand. First printed in 1634, it appears here in its fifth edition of 1658. It is the first English book of conjuring tricks, and it gave the world the phrase hocus pocus, taken from the patter of stage jugglers.

The book explains cups and balls, card tricks, and feats with string and coin. Its aim is exposure as much as teaching: readers learn how the wonders are done. That honesty made it a landmark in the history of stage magic. Generations of conjurers learned their first tricks from its pages. A working manual and a small delight, it still performs its tricks on readers.
